children.text: Cyberskin is a sensor glove and an audio-visual installation. Hand gestures shape generative sound and a 3D point cloud in real time, through a small neural network that reads the state of the hand rather than individual sensor values.

alt: the finished Cyberskin glove: grey ribbed knit with metal studs on the fingers

children.text: Aalok Sud and Alex Bond.
CART 470, Capstone Prototyping, Concordia University. 2026.
Max/MSP, FluCoMa, RAVE (tested), TouchDesigner, OSC, Adafruit LilyPad, a 9-DoF sensor and four bend sensors.
the brief

Cyberskin was our project for CART 470, Capstone Prototyping. We wanted to explore the gap people usually feel between physical objects and technology, and build an installation where a worn object controls a digital environment.
We framed the work with two questions:
How might we turn hand gesture data into a visual and audio environment that feels responsive and personal?
How do we make it avant-garde and expressive enough that the tone is clear the moment someone puts the glove on?
research
Legacy gesture controllers such as the Nintendo Power Glove, for gesture mapping, ergonomics and how immersive a worn controller can feel.
Interactive installations, looking at how physical actions become audio-visual changes, and how visitors engage, where their attention goes and what makes an environment respond.
An interview with a seamstress about fabric choice and pattern making, which set the direction for the first glove prototypes.
audience
who:
people aged roughly 20–30 who are art-forward, comfortable with technology and looking for experiences.
where:
urban exhibitions, public and private.
needs:
immersion, agency (their actions should visibly matter) and awe.
goals
The link between movement and response should feel intuitive and expressive, not mechanical.
The piece should look and feel brutalist and avant-garde, with the hardware visible.
Nothing technical should break the experience while someone is wearing the glove.
how it works

The glove streams 13 values to Max/MSP: four bend sensors (one per finger) and nine axes from the motion sensor. A neural network reduces those 13 values to five parameters, and OSC sends them to the sound engine and to TouchDesigner.
4 bend sensors and a 9-DoF sensor on an Adafruit LilyPad. 13 values.
A FluCoMa neural network (fluid.mlpregressor~) in Max/MSP, trained on example gestures. 13 values in, 5 out.
Frequency, deviate, cutoff, degrade and cycle drive the granular synth and, over OSC, the TouchDesigner point cloud.

children.text: using it
Put the glove on your left hand.
Calibrate by moving through a few gestures.
Move freely: open and close the hand, flex fingers, tilt and shake the wrist.
Grab beats and sounds from the space, and push the point cloud's noise, bloom, orientation and ambience.
key decisions
1. map gestures through a neural network, not one to one
problem.
wiring each sensor to one parameter felt robotic. People ended up operating a controller instead of expressing something.
options.
direct one-to-one mapping; hand-written rules for a few gestures; a trained regression model.
decision.

a FluCoMa multilayer perceptron (fluid.mlpregressor~) trained on a small set of example gestures, such as a relaxed open hand, a clenched fist, a tilt up and a shake. It reads the overall state of the hand (a trembling fist, say) and outputs five parameters at once.
trade-off.
the model needs a short calibration for each wearer, and its output is less predictable than direct mapping.

alt: the FluCoMa training patch in Max/MSP: 13 inputs, a training dataset and 5 target parameters
caption: the FluCoMa training patch: 13 inputs (4 flex + 9 DoF) to 5 outputs

children.text: 2. keep latency under 5ms
problem.
the response has to feel immediate, or the wearer stops believing their hand is doing it.
options.
the RAVE neural audio model; a custom granular synthesis engine in Max/MSP.
decision.
a custom granular engine. RAVE produced interesting textures, but its 50ms latency broke the connection between gesture and sound. The granular engine responds in under 5ms.
trade-off.
we gave up RAVE's more unusual timbres.
3. two layers of sound
problem.
a single sound layer was either too static to feel like an environment or too jumpy to feel calm.
decision.
a continuous textured layer for the environment, plus a rhythmic layer that comes in when the wearer clenches their fist.
4. show the sound as particles breaking apart
problem.
the visuals had to mirror how chaotic the sound was, and show the wearer's effect on the space.
options.
video, still images and several other TouchDesigner node setups, all prototyped before settling.
decision.

3D scans (.obj) converted into a point cloud. A chaos parameter drives a noise operator that blows the particles apart, and a feedback loop leaves trails so the visuals fade out with the sound instead of stopping dead.
trade-off.
the scans are existing models. We plan to make our own.

alt: the TouchDesigner network: scans switch into a point cloud, then displacement, feedback, noise and bloom
caption: TouchDesigner: 10 scans → switch → geo → point cloud → render → displace → feedback → noise → bloom → OSC mapping

children.text: 5. a stretchy knit glove that fits many hands
problem.
an installation glove is worn by many people with different hand sizes.
decision.

a stretchy grey ribbed knit from Tonitex, a Montreal fabric warehouse, chosen for elasticity and comfort. The pattern went through several versions, adjusting finger length, curve and width, before cutting the front and back pieces. Straps were added to hold the microcontroller and bend sensors.
trade-off.
the knit is delicate for a piece handled by the public.

children.text: 6. leave the hardware visible
problem.
the circuit could be hidden or made soft.
options.
embroider the circuit with conductive thread; keep the raw hardware on show.
decision.
keep the hardware visible, in line with the brutalist direction.
trade-off.
exposed solder joints are fragile.
7. remove ghost data
problem.
sensors shifting inside the fabric sent signals the wearer didn't intend, which made the visuals jump.
decision.
a software low-pass filter (slide~) smooths the signal, every sensor module is tacked down between the fabric layers, and every solder joint was tested for continuity and noise.
trade-off.
smoothing adds a little lag, which we kept well inside the latency budget.
testing
We tested the glove on a range of people. Their feedback, and the bugs they found, fed into the calibration step, the signal smoothing and how firmly the sensors are held in place.

children.text: next steps
installation:
drape fabric and project onto it, ideally in a dark room.
a sturdier glove:
a more self-supporting material, such as a down-filled puffer with a clear plastic panel that shows the circuit but protects it.
circuit:
redesign the most delicate solder joints.
visuals:
scan and curate our own models for the point clouds.
